What if the people businesses are reluctant to hire are some of the talent they’re missing out on? There can be a perception that employing someone who has experienced homelessness, or is at risk of it, will require more time, support and investment. , CEO ofand UK Chair of Homewards’ New Employment Opportunities Network, believes employers should look at the other side of that equation. With the right recruitment, onboarding and ongoing support, businesses can open themselves up to a more diverse pool of talent, help people stay and progress in work and strengthen retention. That matters to individual businesses. But it matters to the economy too. With around one in eight young people not in education, employment or training, businesses have an opportunity to be part of the solution by giving people who might otherwise be overlooked a genuine route into sustainable work. NEON exists to help make that easier, connecting employers to local organisations that support both the business and the young person before and after they start work. sat down withto discuss why this isn’t simply about social responsibility. It’s about seeing potential where others see risk. Full episode in the comments 👇 Follow, hosted by, for conversations about the future of work and careers nobody else is having. … more

30 Sekunden Video. Und plötzlich fallen Scammer und Blender durchs Raster. Bevor ein Kandidat einen unserer Kunden trifft, gibt es in unserem Auswahlprozess einen einfachen ersten Schritt: ein 30-Sekunden-Video über sich. Nicht zur Präsentation beim Kunden. Nicht, um das Aussehen zu beurteilen. Und schon gar nicht als Ersatz für die technische Prüfung. Es geht um Kommunikation. In verteilten Engineering-Teams ist technisches Können nur ein Teil der Gleichung. Man muss eine technische Entscheidung klar erklären können, ein Problem ansprechen, bevor es zum Blocker wird, die richtigen Fragen stellen und komplexe Themen für Menschen verständlich machen, die nicht denselben fachlichen Hintergrund haben. Das zeigt kein Lebenslauf. Und ein Coding-Test zeigt es auch nicht zuverlässig. Das Video leistet außerdem etwas, womit wir anfangs nicht gerechnet haben: Es filtert früh. Wir haben schon Kandidaten im Bademantel oder Schlafanzug im Interview gehabt. Wir hatten Bewerber, die angaben, in der EU zu leben und geboren zu sein, aber keine einzige EU-Landessprache beherrschten und ihre Antworten von einem zweiten Bildschirm ablasen. Es geht uns nicht um Hochglanz. Aber Professionalität und ein echtes Gespräch zählen, und 30 Sekunden reichen oft, um zu sehen, ob beides da ist. Wer diesen Schritt besteht, bekommt von uns mehr: Jeder Kandidat erhält ein auf die jeweilige Stelle zugeschnittenes Vorbereitungsdokument und ein weiteres persönliches Gespräch mit uns, damit er gut vorbereitet und entspannt ins finale Kundengespräch geht. Denn in Teams, die über Länder, Zeitzonen und Kulturen hinweg arbeiten, ist Kommunikation kein Soft Skill. Es ist ein absolutes Must-Have. Bei Scorpion Power, Teil der POWERCODE GROUP, nutzen wir strukturierte Auswahlverfahren, um Engineers zu finden, die technisch überzeugen und in verteilten Teams gut kommunizieren. 30 Sekunden zeigen oft mehr, als ein Lebenslauf je könnte. Najlepiej przygotowane organizacje nie muszą być tymi, które wydają najwięcej. Kluczowe jest zrozumienie, co należy chronić, jakie ryzyka mogą zagrozić działalności oraz czy wdrożone zabezpieczenia rzeczywiście działają. Kiedy zarząd ostatnio rozmawiał o ryzyku cybernetycznym obok ryzyka płynności lub kredytowego? NIS2 is more than another regulatory obligation. It is an opportunity to treat cybersecurity as a core element of business resilience, alongside liquidity, credit risk and going concern. The best-prepared organisations will not necessarily be those that spend the most. What matters is understanding what needs to be protected, which risks could disrupt the business and whether the safeguards in place actually work. The U.S. Job Market Is Moving, But Hiring Is Still a Challenge There's something interesting happening in the U.S. job market. Recent ADP data shows that private employers added 86,000 jobs in October, which is better than many economists expected. That's encouraging, but I don't think the bigger story is just the number of jobs being added. Companies are still being careful about who they hire. Many businesses want experienced people who can step in, understand the work, and contribute without a long learning curve. At the same time, job seekers are facing a different kind of challenge. Having experience doesn't always mean finding the right opportunity is easy. I think employers need to look beyond a resume and pay more attention to practical skills, adaptability, and the ability to work with others. A strong business isn't built by hiring the most people. It's built by bringing in the right people. For those involved in hiring, what's harder today: finding qualified candidates or finding people who are the right fit for the company? #USJobMarket #Hiring #CareerDevelopment #BusinessLeadership #HumanResources #Employment … more

A gap on your CV isn't the problem. An unexplained gap is. Humans have this psychological quirk where we fill gaps in information with the worst-case scenario. Many contractors, especially, take lengthier breaks between demanding projects to live their lives: spend time with family, travel, develop their skills. It might seem silly or unprofessional to include this on your CV, but, if a hiring manager has never spoken to you, a blank stretch on your CV can become 'couldn’t find work' or 'left on bad terms', when the reality is usually different. You may have been working toward professional qualifications, building relationships for future work, travelling, honing soft skills. But, the hiring manager won't know unless you tell them: ❌ [blank gap, Mar 2025 – Oct 2025] ✅ Career break, Mar 2025 – Oct 2025: completed CISI qualification in July and spent time with family. (Swap in what’s true for you. Don’t invent anything, because it’ll come up at interview.) Keep it short, honest and confident. This context and proactive attitude is what separates the shining CVs from the dim ones. U.S. Job Cuts Fall to Lowest October Since 2023 U.S. employers announced 43,994 job cuts in October, down 71% from a year earlier and the lowest October total since 2023, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Inc. Through the first 10 months of 2026, announced cuts total 617,189, down 44% from the same period last year and the lowest year-to-date figure since 2022. Challenger's figures track employer announcements rather than completed layoffs, making them an early indicator of corporate employment decisions rather than an official measure of job losses. While the national numbers suggest a more stable labor market, the industry breakdown reveals a much more uneven picture, with food companies leading October at 9,677 announced cuts, followed by technology at 5,576 and services at 5,458. Technology still accounts for 28% of all announced cuts this year, while food-industry cuts are up 43%, transportation cuts have increased 188%, and FinTech cuts are up 543%. The national improvement is significant, but it does not mean every industry is experiencing a healthier labor market. That unevenness also extends to hiring, with employers announcing plans to hire 444,692 workers in October, up 57% from a year earlier and the highest October total since at least 2009. However, Amazon and UPS accounted for 400,000 of those planned positions, nearly 90% of the total, and both announcements were for seasonal employment. Just five companies have announced seasonal hiring plans this year compared with 11 last year, while retailers announced 3,692 job cuts in October even as they planned to hire 13,300 workers. The reasons for layoffs are changing as well, with market and economic conditions accounting for 37% of October's announced cuts, compared with just 1,265 attributed to artificial intelligence. Economic conditions have now overtaken AI as the leading stated reason for job reductions this year, suggesting that broader economic pressures are becoming more prominent even as overall layoff announcements remain relatively low. Taken together with this week's JOLTS and ADP reports, these findings reinforce the distinction between job security and job opportunity, but I think the industry differences deserve more attention. The national labor market can look healthier while workers in industries experiencing continued layoffs see little reason for optimism, particularly if they believe finding another comparable job would be difficult. Two households with similar incomes can therefore have very different expectations about their financial futures simply because they work in different industries, and those expectations can influence spending decisions long before either household experiences an actual loss of income. For Havas Edge, understanding where employment is improving and where uncertainty persists helps explain why consumer spending behavior can differ so significantly across households. … more

Remote Work Is a Skillset Too… Being good at your technical job does not automatically mean you are good at remote work. Remote experience is useful, but it isn’t the only way to demonstrate remote-work readiness. Candidates can build credible proof by showing how they communicate, organize tasks, use workplace tools, solve problems, and work independently. A simple portfolio might include: • A professional email • A mock project tracker • A customer-support response • A short screen-recorded process walkthrough Examples from retail, school, volunteering, caregiving, freelancing, and personal projects can also support your case. Describe the situation, your actions, and the result. Add metrics only when they’re accurate. Finally, tailor that proof to the posting. Look for repeated requirements such as written communication, customer service, spreadsheets, scheduling, data entry, troubleshooting, CRM systems, or ticketing tools. We’re approaching 2027, and some technology companies are STILL insisting that employees show up to the office. I have two female friends whose jobs are very similar to mine. Their work requires nothing more than a laptop, a Wi-Fi connection, and a reliable internet connection to operate. Yet, their companies require them to be in the office at least 3 days a week. Both are mothers. So, their mornings look something like this: • Get the kids ready. • Drop them off at daycare. • Commute to the office. • Spend the day doing a job they could have done from anywhere. • Repeat. The result? At least 15% of their salaries goes towards childcare, not to mention commuting costs, commuting time, and the additional pressure on their daily lives. Can we please stop giving remote-work bashers more ammunition? I keep seeing posts from people working from home focusing on the downsides, like getting distracted by housework or all the jobs that need doing around the house. Remote working gets enough of a bad rap without people fortunate enough to have that flexibility adding to it! Some of the comments are unbelievable. People openly admitting they’re watching TV instead of working. Of course, it happens sometimes, but actually putting that in writing on LinkedIn? Really?! And we wonder why some employers want people back in the office! Apparently, everyone's either laying on a beach or doing yoga on a cliff. 😂 The reality is, most normal hard working people are just getting on with their jobs at home. Everyone works differently. When I worked for a company I had a dedicated office and stuck to office hours. You’re not worrying about getting home in time for after-school club (or doggy day care) pick-up or missing the train. Yes, people can go for a walk at lunchtime and probably have more coffee breaks than they would in an office. So what?! I’m a huge advocate for remote working because I know how productive it made me without the noise and distractions of a busy office or the stress of a commute. Candidates, please stop making this mistake. We ask a candidate: “What is your current salary?” They tell us their number, then immediately say: “I know it’s high, and I don’t mind taking less.” Wait… why? How did you decide that your salary is high before even knowing the salary range for the new role? In many cases, the range offered by the employer is actually higher than what the candidate is currently earning. Don’t negotiate against yourself. First, understand the role, responsibilities, market value, and the employer’s salary range. Then have a conversation about compensation. You might be willing to take less for the right opportunity, and that’s completely fine. But don’t offer to lower your salary before anyone even asks you to. Know your value. Ask questions. And never assume you’re being paid too much without knowing what the opportunity actually offers. … more

Salary won't be someone's only consideration. However, knowing whether a role meets their financial needs helps them decide whether to explore it further. For hiring firms, leaving out the salary could mean missing an application from someone with the experience you need. It also creates an extra step for candidates who want to clarify pay before applying. Since 1935, federal law has protected most private-sector employees' right to discuss their pay. And about half of American workers still say their employer prohibits or discourages it. So most people never learn how to bring it up. Here’s a playbook. 1. Start with your own number. In most private-sector jobs, you can share your own pay. Nobody has to share theirs. 2. Ask for the range, not the salary. “Do you know the range for this role?” In Massachusetts, employers with 25 or more employees have to give you the range for your own position when you ask. 3. Compare roles, not people. “What’s a fair range for a Senior Accountant at a company like ours?” It’s easier to answer, and it gets you the same information. 4. Ask before the offer, not after. 17% of applicants who saw a posted range were later offered below it (Patriot Software, 2026). Ask where in the range the offer lands, and why. 5. Then actually ask. The worst answer is no. The best answer is more money. Most people never find out which one they would have gotten. Talking about pay isn’t gossip. It’s information. GTK #6 💡 Find out what the research reveals: Researchers analyzed 10 million job postings and conducted one field experiment and two lab experiments to investigate how salary ranges influence job applications and negotiations. They found that women were more likely than men to prefer jobs with narrow salary ranges rather than wide ones. For example: - Narrow salary range: 55.000€ – 75.000€ - Wide salary range: 40.000€ – 90.000€ They were therefore also less likely to negotiate, and ultimately asked for lower salaries. In other words, the width of salary ranges in job postings can unintentionally disadvantage women. But there is a simple way to prevent this effect. When recruiters explained the typical starting salary and how the final salary would be determined: For example: “The typical starting salary is around €65,000. Your exact salary offer will reflect your relevant experience, skill level, and the responsibilities of the role, in line with our standardized compensation guidelines.” - Women's preference for jobs with wide salary ranges increased from 48.5% to 60.3%, reaching the same level as men's. - The difference between men and women in salary negotiations also disappeared. 🤨 Why? - Wide salary ranges create uncertainty about what candidates can realistically expect to earn. - Women are generally more risk-averse than men, making wide salary ranges less attractive to them. - Explaining the typical starting salary and how pay is determined reduces that uncertainty, making wider salary ranges more appealing. 👇 What can recruiters do? Don't just disclose salary ranges. Explain them. When posting a job, specify: - The typical starting salary for candidates meeting the core requirements. - How experience, skills and responsibilities influence the final salary offer. “What are your salary expectations?” Five words that can make a job seeker suddenly forget how to speak. Do you give a figure immediately? Do you ask what the company has budgeted? Do you say you're open to negotiation? I've realised that answering this question shouldn't be based on guesswork. Before applying for a role, I believe it's important to understand the value of the position and the compensation being offered. Here are a few things I'm paying more attention to: 💰 1. Research the market. Look at salary ranges for similar roles, considering the country, industry, experience level, and type of company. 🌍 2. Consider the location. A remote role with a company in Nigeria may have a different compensation structure from one hiring internationally. Don't assume every remote job pays the same. 📌 3. Understand the responsibilities. A Junior Frontend Developer and a Senior Frontend Engineer shouldn't automatically have the same salary expectations. 🧮 4. Know your own range. Have a realistic minimum and target figure in mind before the interview. 🤝 5. Be prepared to negotiate. Your answer should communicate flexibility without making it seem like you haven't considered your value. One way to approach the question is: "Based on my understanding of the role, its responsibilities, and the market range, I have a compensation range in mind. However, I'm open to discussing the budget allocated for the position and the overall benefits." Of course, I'd adjust that answer depending on the role and whether the employer has already disclosed a salary range. I'm learning that salary conversations are easier when you've done your research before entering the room. Who sees your pay ranges first: the candidate who applied yesterday, or the employee who's been with you for three years? Most companies are getting this wrong. In Pave's 2027 report, 80.2% of companies post a salary range on every US job ad. But inside those same companies: - Only 13.9% make an employee's own range automatically available. 43.4% share it on request. 20.5% don't share it at all. So at most companies, a candidate can read a version of the range before an employee can see theirs without asking. I understand how we got here. Candidate transparency arrived through legislation. Conversely, employee transparency is a choice, and most companies haven't really made it yet. But your employees read your job ads too. (and I see this hurt companies all the time) If the ad is the first place someone sees their band, you've lost the chance to explain it. (And "on request" asks people to put their hand up about their own pay, which many may not do.) How I'd give employees at least the same experience as candidates: → Put each person's band in your HRIS, plus the level above → Explain how the bands were built and where you target in the market → Define what each position in the range means → Brief managers before it goes live Your employees should never know less about pay than the people you're trying to hire. In 11 months, I negotiated $71K to $153K as a data analyst in tech My secret is shutting your mouth and not saying any numbers. I never would’ve thought I was worth $140K-153K, so I probably wouldn’t have asked for that much… but multiple companies willingly offered it to me! I realized that saying a number first was me doing their job for them. I was basically telling them exactly how little they could pay me without negotiating. And this way, I was definitely going to lowball myself. Because their budget is almost always more than you think it is. So I stopped saying numbers. Every time a recruiter asked "what are your salary expectations?" I'd say: "I'd love to meet with more members of the team and better understand the role so I can assess the market value. But if you have a budget, I wouldn't mind hearing it.” Then SIT IN THE SILENCE. Don’t fill the awkwardness. Just wait for them to talk. Silence is your power, own it. Companies will almost tell you their budget and if they don’t thats a red flag. Once they named their number, I either said yes, I'm aligned with that range or I moved on. Good negotiation skills literally make you money over time not just in your salary but in your %-based bonuses and raises, 401K contributions, and compounding interest 💅🏻 … more

A posted pay range sets expectations before your recruiter says a word. Ogletree's update on New Jersey's proposed pay-transparency rules is a useful prompt to review the posting itself. The regulatory changes discussed are proposals; the state's pay and benefits disclosure law is already in effect. From the candidate's side, the range helps answer a basic question: is this opportunity worth pursuing? If the conversation later reveals a much narrower budget or different compensation, the candidate has to reassess after investing time in the process. The article's employer questions make a useful checklist: - Does the posting show clear minimum and maximum pay? - Are benefits and other compensation described? - Do recruiter and job-board versions provide consistent information? - Can applicants reach linked disclosures without unnecessary hurdles? - Are current employees hearing about promotional opportunities? I would add a question for the recruiter and hiring manager: what would place someone at different points in the range, and does the approved hiring budget support that explanation (and the range)? A broad salary band can encompass progression over a career. The job posting needs to help candidates understand this particular opening. Before publishing, read it as a candidate. But let's not confuse negotiation with applying for an opportunity you already know doesn't align with your expectations. So candidates, please read the advert before applying. 💫Pay transparency isn't just about compliance💫 Most employers say they want to pay people fairly. Fewer are fully confident that their own pay arrangements would hold up if someone looked closely.⬇️ Over time, organisations change. Roles grow, businesses merge and salaries get agreed in very different markets. Each decision might have made sense at the time. Taken together, they can be hard to explain. The EU Pay Transparency Directive and the government's recent consultation on equal pay are bringing this into the open. Our autumn Reward Management Survey suggests it's already changing how organisations think about pay, with an increased push for transparency. Why is one role paid more than another? Why are two people doing similar jobs on different salaries? What determines whether someone progresses to the next pay grade? These aren't unreasonable questions. Employees are already asking the questions. Why is my role paid less than that one? Why are two of us doing similar work on different salaries? Publishing pay ranges won't answer those questions by itself. You need a clear, consistent basis for how jobs are valued and that's what job evaluation gives you. It isn't the most exciting topic on the HR agenda but I would argue it's one of the most important right now. You don't have to fix everything at once. A headhunter ended our conversation after just 30 seconds. I was still a young woman at the time, working in an office when I received a call from a headhunter’s secretary. We arranged a phone conversation for 11:00 a.m. The headhunter was supposed to call me. At 11:05 a.m., I still hadn’t heard from him. So I decided to call him myself. He sounded annoyed: “I would have called you.” He was an older gentleman, very direct, factual and straight to the point. Then, without any introduction, he asked: “What are your salary expectations?” I wasn’t prepared for that question. I hesitated for a moment and eventually said €50,000 ??! gross per year. And honestly, I was thinking to myself: I hope that’s not too much! 😬 His response came immediately: “Thank you. This conversation is over.” And he hung up. I was completely stunned. My first thought was: What an idiot! But then I started researching the position and eventually found the original job advertisement on his website. The advertised salary range was €70,000 to €90,000 per year. And suddenly, I understood. I hadn’t asked for too much. I had asked for far too little. 🤦‍♀️ So… Even when you’re impatient, it’s still better to be patient, wait rather than trying to force results… and coming across as insecure won’t get you the job you want. 😉 #Recruitment #CareerAdvice #Nigeria #RemoteJobs #CareerDevelopment … more

I was scrolling through LinkedIn when Netflix casually announced a job paying up to $605,000, and I almost dropped coffee into another tax bracket. Director of Security & Intelligence. SIX HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS. For that kind of money, I expect the candidate to protect the building, interrogate the Wi-Fi, and personally wrestle every hacker into the opening credits. But naturally, Netflix has requirements. An advanced degree in security. Ten plus years of increasing responsibility at a multinational entertainment studio. Prior leadership overseeing studio security. So basically, they’re hiring Batman, but only if Gotham was a subsidiary of Warner Bros. and Bruce Wayne submitted his transcripts. Imagine having 20 years of military intelligence experience, stopping actual threats, protecting world leaders, and being told, “Unfortunately, your background isn’t sufficiently entertainment focused.” Sorry, General. You may have prevented an international crisis, but have you ever secured a trailer for a reality show about people marrying strangers through a wall? And the salary range? $352,000 to $605,000, all in. You can choose salary versus stock options. No bonus. Oh, the sacrifice! How will this poor executive survive without a bonus? Should we start a GoFundMe? I want to see the interview process. Round one: recruiter screening. Round two: panel. Round three: personality assessment. Round four: explain a gap in your resume from 2009. Round five: stop a simulated cyberattack while the hiring manager asks where you see yourself in five years. Round six: a one way video where you describe your greatest weakness to an empty screen. Round seven: protect the CEO from a rogue Netflix recommendation. “Why Netflix?” “Because apparently you’re paying enough for me to buy the entire neighborhood and install a moat.” “Are you comfortable working in a fast paced environment?” “Ma’am, I once evacuated a stadium.” “Yes, but can you handle feedback from a vice president who calls every meeting a sync?” And let’s talk about the title: Security & Intelligence. Will this person finally investigate who keeps canceling shows after one season? Because THAT is the cold case America needs solved. Forget encrypted files. Find the executive who looked at a beloved series and said, “Interesting. Yes, Netflix. I’m still watching. It’s Saturday. I’m wearing sweatpants. You have no moral authority here. Of course, the actual work may be serious and the compensation may reflect that. But the job post reads like they want the head of the CIA, a Hollywood producer, and Batman stacked inside one trench coat. A candidate can like your company, accept the salary range and still turn down your offer because of the medical benefits. That’s why benchmarking your PEO needs to go deeper than the monthly price. Start with these five things: → Network Are their doctors, specialists and hospitals in it? The same insurance carrier can offer different networks. → Coinsurance After meeting the deductible, how much of the bill does the employee still pay? → Maximum out-of-pocket What could an employee or family have to spend in a bad medical year? What falls outside that limit? → Deductible How much do they pay before the plan starts sharing costs, and which services are covered before that? → Premium What do the company and employee each pay every month? Then check prescription coverage, copays and out-of-network benefits. Those details can change the comparison considerably. Imagine saving an employee $100 a month in premiums while increasing their deductible by $3,000. You’ve lowered their fixed cost. You may also have increased what they’ll spend when they need care. Understand where the savings come from. And remember who has to live with the decision. A candidate whose specialist isn’t in the network or whose child’s medication isn’t covered may choose another employer. Your existing employees are making those comparisons too. At Dinsmore Steele®, we compare the medical offerings alongside the costs so you can see what you’re gaining, what you’re giving up and whether the trade makes sense. A cheaper PEO isn’t a better deal if the savings make your job offers harder to accept. If you are a foreigner applying for jobs in Singapore and the replies stop after the first message, or you keep wondering whether your nationality is the problem, this is worth reading. I review CVs from professionals applying to Singapore from abroad as well as from people who have just relocated, and the same few gaps keep turning up. In most of them, the issue was not the experience or the passport. It was positioning: nothing on the page told the employer that hiring this person was a practical option. Three things I keep finding: 1️⃣ The role cannot pay enough for a work pass. The Employment Pass has a minimum monthly salary that rises with age, starting from $5,600 now and from $6,000 for new applications from 1 January 2027. If the advertised range tops out below the minimum for your age, the employer cannot hire you on that pass, however strong your CV is. 2️⃣ Page one does not say where you are or when you can start. A common version: a strong CV with no location, no notice period and no mention of Singapore. The employer has to guess how soon you could join, so they move on to someone they do not have to guess about. 3️⃣ Employers are described only for a home-country reader. “Regional Manager at [company]” means little to a hiring manager here who has never heard of it. One line on markets, headcount or scale fixes that. What works better: • Check the salary range against the pass minimum for your age before you apply • Put “Relocating to Singapore, available from [month]”, or your current pass status, under your name • Add one line of scale to every employer you list If you are applying to Singapore from abroad and want to know what an employer here sees first on your CV, send it over and I will tell you. … more

It's a live debate right now, not a hypothetical one. The UK government is currently consulting on requiring employers to publish pay information in job adverts, with that consultation closing 27 October. The proposal on the table is narrower than people sometimes assume — pay and conditions information in job adverts, or before interview if there isn't one, rather than the broader pay-equity rules some EU countries have introduced. The detail that matters most — how wide a pay range is allowed to be — has deliberately been left to future regulation. You don't need to wait for legislation to make this decision. Around 21.6% of UK employers already publish pay information in their adverts voluntarily — meaning most still don't, but a meaningful minority have already concluded it's worth doing regardless of what the law eventually requires. From where I sit, hiding the number rarely protects an employer — it just means you find out a candidate's expectations don't match yours at offer stage, several interview rounds too late. Publishing a realistic range filters out mismatched applications before they start. The genuine concern isn't transparency itself — it's publishing a range before you're confident it's the right one, and then finding it hard to move off it later. If you ask for my current salary, share your budget first. In almost every interview or LinkedIn message, HR asks: "What's your current salary?" But when the candidate asks: "What's the budget for this role?", the answer is usually: "We'll discuss it later" or "It depends on your experience." Let's be honest. Every company already has an approved salary range for the position before they even post the job. The budget exists. It's not a secret to them, only to the candidate. So why does the current salary matter? Too often, it's used as an anchor. Instead of paying what the role is worth, the offer is based on what the person earned before, usually just above their current package and close to the minimum of the range. That's not fair, for a few reasons: A salary should reflect the role, responsibilities, and value you bring, not your last company's pay scale. Someone who was underpaid before shouldn't stay underpaid forever. Negotiation only works when both sides share information. Right now, one side shows all its cards and the other shows none. My simple suggestion to HR and recruiters: Share the salary range early, ideally in the job post or the first call. If you ask for the candidate's current salary, be ready to share your budget too. Make offers based on the role and the candidate's skills, not their salary history. Transparency builds trust. Candidates who feel respected during hiring become employees who stay. My suggestion for all candidates: it's okay to politely ask, "Could you share the budgeted range for this role?" You deserve to know. What do you think? Listened in on a Talent Acquisition roundtable this morning, and heard about a hiring trend that is completely defeating the purpose of pay transparency: Employers weaponizing compensation asks against candidates who ask for a number squarely inside the posted salary range. If you advertise a salary range, but immediately disqualify an applicant the moment they target the upper half of it, you did not post a range in good faith. While employers retain discretion over final offers, using salary requests within an advertised band as a screening gate runs dangerously afoul of both the letter and the spirit of labor statutes: The "Good Faith" Mandate: Pay transparency laws across California (SB 1162 / SB 642), New York State (Labor Law § 194-b), Washington State (RCW 49.58.110), Colorado (Equal Pay for Equal Work Act), and Illinois mandate that employers post a bona fide, good-faith wage scale that the organization genuinely intends and is budgeted to pay at hire. If the top 30% of your band is purely decorative and triggering disqualifications, that posted range is materially misleading and vulnerable to regulatory audit and statutory penalties. Salary History Bans & Screen-Out Protections: Over 22 states and numerous cities (e.g., California Labor Code § 432.3, New York, Illinois) explicitly make it unlawful to screen applicants based on past compensation or refuse to interview/hire based on prior wage metrics. When companies push candidates into compensation corners early to disqualify them, they risk creating pretextual rejections that invite disparate impact scrutiny. Pay Equity & Discrimination Exposure (Title VII / Equal Pay Acts): Weaponizing salary asks often disproportionately impact underrepresented groups. Studies consistently demonstrate that women and marginalized professionals are penalized more harshly during compensation discussions. Posting an inflated band just to attract top-tier talent, only to filter out anyone who takes you at your word is bait-and-switch recruiting. Pay transparency wasn't passed so organizations could check a compliance box while preserving information asymmetry. It was passed to create level, transparent negotiations. Candidate screening should be about competence, impact, and culture add: not a guessing game where naming an approved number disqualifies you. Let's do better! #PayTransparency #HiringEthics #Recruiting #EqualPay #HumanResources #TalentAcquisition … more

We need to acknowledge that not everyone looking for employment is financially comfortable. Some people are unemployed, struggling to meet basic needs, yet are expected to keep investing in their job search. Now, on to another issue: salary transparency. Why advertise a job vacancy without disclosing the salary or at least providing a salary range? I genuinely believe employers should include compensation details in their job advertisements. Let an adult decide whether the proposed salary is worth their time, skills, experience and effort. If the budget is fixed, state it. If the salary is negotiable depending on experience, communicate that too. Job seekers deserve the opportunity to make informed decisions before investing their time in lengthy application processes and interviews. Transparency saves time for both the employer and the applicant. We cannot keep telling people to value their skills, negotiate better and know their worth while making it unnecessarily difficult for them to understand what an opportunity actually offers. Companies Want Salary Transparency During Hiring, But Not Among Employees! Dear Corporate India, let's talk about another interesting corporate practice. 🤔 During recruitment, the first few questions are usually: What's your current CTC? What's your expected CTC? How much are you willing to negotiate? Do you have any competing offers? Companies want complete transparency when it comes to understanding how much they need to pay you. But when employees discuss their salaries with colleagues? Suddenly, it's considered inappropriate! Why this double standard? Let's understand a few uncomfortable realities: 📌 Same role, different salaries: Two employees with similar qualifications, experience and responsibilities may receive significantly different compensation. 📌 Salary confidentiality: Employees are often discouraged from discussing their compensation with colleagues. 📌 Unequal negotiation power: Employees who negotiate aggressively during recruitment may secure better packages than those who don't. 📌 Existing employees vs new hires: Sometimes, a newly hired employee earns more than someone who has been contributing to the organisation for years. 📌 Lack of transparency: Employees often have no clear understanding of how salary structures, increments and compensation bands work. Now, let's be fair. Not every salary difference is discrimination. Experience, performance, specialised skills, responsibilities and market conditions can justify differences. But shouldn't employees at least have some clarity about how compensation decisions are made? If two employees perform similar roles, shouldn't there be a transparent and reasonable basis for their compensation differences? Companies cannot expect employees to negotiate confidently during recruitment while discouraging conversations that help them understand their market value. And here's something worth thinking about: Salary secrecy doesn't automatically create salary fairness. Transparency can help employees identify inequalities and encourage organisations to address them. 💬 Let's discuss: Do you think employees should openly discuss their salaries with colleagues, or should compensation remain confidential? 15 interviews. 8 leading companies. 4 months. The past four months have given me a new perspective on Finland’s engineering job market. Following my time at GE HealthCare, I began exploring opportunities in electronics manufacturing, test engineering, automation, and quality engineering. What followed was approximately 15 interviews across 8 well-established companies operating in Finland. When I shared these numbers with a few friends, some were genuinely surprised. I hadn’t thought much about the numbers myself. I was simply focused on the next opportunity. The journey included technical assessments, multiple interview rounds, discussions with hiring managers, some disappointments, and a few job offers. Not every offer aligned with my salary expectations or career goals, which taught me something important: Finding a job and finding the right job are two different things. One topic that stood out was salary transparency. Going through several interview rounds only to discover that compensation expectations differ significantly can be frustrating for both candidates and employers. That’s why I welcome the EU Pay Transparency Directive and the conversation around making salary information available earlier in recruitment. Personally, I believe salary ranges in job advertisements would help both sides make more informed decisions. Beyond that, this experience made me appreciate how much goes into a job search that we rarely talk about. We often celebrate the final outcome, but behind it are countless hours of preparation, uncertainty, difficult decisions, and personal growth. I’m particularly grateful to the recruiters, hiring managers, career coaches, and friends who offered their time, encouragement, and feedback along the way. I also recognize that many talented professionals in Finland are facing much tougher circumstances. My experience is just one perspective, not a reflection of everyone’s reality. I’ve gathered dozens of practical lessons throughout this journey and hope to share some in future posts, while respecting the confidentiality of recruitment processes. A few questions worth discussing: • Should salary ranges be included in all job advertisements? • How can employers provide more constructive feedback to candidates? • Beyond salary, what makes an opportunity worth accepting or declining? Transparency and confidentiality don’t have to be mutually exclusive. We often talk about where people end up. Perhaps we should talk a little more about what happens along the way. #Finland #JobMarket #Engineering #Recruitment #SalaryTransparency … more

In case you missed it… Last week the EHRC called to an end of salary secrecy! The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) released a clear set of recommendations calling for an overhaul of the UK equal pay framework. Among them: giving workers the right to request salary details for colleagues performing similar work and officially banning salary history queries during recruitment. It mirrors the direction of travel we are seeing with the EU Pay Transparency Directive, and it highlights how quickly administrative pay secrecy is collapsing globally. Historically, many reward models relied heavily on opacity. Using a candidate's prior salary as the baseline for a new offer simply anchored legacy disparities into new compensation structures. At Amazon, we have had a global ban on requesting prior salary details for a number of years. In practice, removing that metric forces hiring mechanisms to focus strictly on objective job pricing, internal equity, and the candidate’s actual capability rather than historical negotiation leverage. Waiting for legislation to force change is usually a sign of reactive governance. When you proactively eliminate salary history queries and build clear, objective range architectures, the operational benefits are immediate: - Offer acceptance and candidate trust increase because roles are priced on internal value, not historical pay. - Internal mobility becomes far cleaner as employees understand the exact capability thresholds required for progression. - Pay compression and equity risks are caught and resolved before they turn into systemic liabilities. Pay transparency is shifting from a compliance obligation to a core operational trust mechanism. Pay transparency laws in 2026 now require you to defend every salary on your books, not just job postings. The shift matters. Job-ad transparency is table stakes. Internal pay structure transparency is different. A regulator or employee can now ask why Person A in the same role makes 18% more than Person B, and "that's what we hired them at" doesn't close the gap. The compression risk Neil Vicente flagged in Thomson Reuters' latest Payroll Pulse is real. You don't have to pay everyone the same. You do have to articulate why the differences exist. Experience gap. Promotion timing. Scope creep in the role. Market adjustment when you hired. Performance differential tied to documented outcomes. Those hold up. Gut feel doesn't. For founders and HR-of-one operators running 25 to 500 people, this means an audit before the question arrives. Pull your current roster. Map title to comp. Ask yourself: could I explain this to a lawyer? If the answer is no, you have a comp debt problem that's no longer theoretical. This isn't about compression for its own sake. It's about having a system that survives scrutiny. The companies getting ahead aren't the ones paying everyone equally. They're the ones who can document the logic. What's your current comp structure based on? Title, tenure, market data, performance, or some combination nobody wrote down? #paytransparency #compensation #peopleops #compliance … more

Have you ever heard one of these phrases at the dinner table, at work or in the comments? Save this post, here’s how to respond next time. “It’s because women work fewer hours.” Our figure measures the hourly pay gap: it compares one hour of a woman’s work with one hour of a man’s. So even if everyone worked full-time, the gap would still exist. “It’s because they look after the children.” Exactly: the gap widens after the birth of the first child, as Nobel Prize-winning economist Claudia Goldin has shown, for mothers but not fathers. It’s not that women’s work is worth less; it’s that the burden of care is still unequally distributed. Nearly 30% of employed women work part-time, compared with 8% of men, and a third of them do so involuntarily (INSEE). “They just need to negotiate.” You can only negotiate effectively when you have the information. Without pay transparency, women don’t know the salary range for a position or how much their colleagues earn. This is precisely what the European Pay Transparency Directive is designed to change. “That’s not true. Give me an example.” Here’s one: 87% of nursing staff are women, with an average gross monthly salary of around €2,500, while 72% of police officers are men, earning around €3,300. And when teaching was a predominantly male profession, teachers’ average salary was close to the median wage. It has since fallen to around 75% of it. “The gap is only 4% for the same job.” That 4% represents the share of the pay gap that cannot be explained by anything other than gender. “Competitive salary” isn’t a salary. Put the range in the job advert. Three interview rounds is too long to wait to hear the number. By the time pay comes up, a candidate may have taken time off work, paid for transport across Lagos twice, prepared a case study and sat through a panel. Then the offer comes in below what they earn now, and everyone has lost a month. Employers lose too. The role goes back to market after the final round, and the candidates with the most options often skip adverts that don’t say what the job pays. The usual objections don’t hold up well. “It weakens our negotiating position.” A range still leaves room to negotiate. It just starts the conversation in the right place. “Our current staff will see it.” If your team would be upset to see what a new hire could earn, the advert didn’t create that problem. It only made it visible. “Everyone will ask for the top of the range.” Some will. That’s what the interviews are for. Parts of Europe are making it law. The EU Pay Transparency Directive requires employers to give candidates the starting pay or range, in the advert or before the first interview, and stops them asking about pay history. Countries were due to adopt it by June 2026, and only four had fully done so by the deadline, so even there it’s moving slowly. We don’t need a directive to start. If you’re hiring, put the range in the advert. You’ll probably get fewer applications, and more of the right ones. If you’re applying, ask for the range on the first call. A company that won’t share it before round three has already told you something. … more

Want to know what your colleagues earn? You might soon have the right to find out. 👀 And I think greater pay transparency could be a VERY good thing. The Equality and Human Rights Commission has recommended giving employees a legal right to request relevant pay information where they suspect pay discrimination. It's also calling for employers to publish salaries on job adverts AND stop asking candidates about their previous salary. YES. 👏 Because I've never understood why what somebody earned in their LAST job should determine what they're worth in their NEXT one. Imagine two candidates applying for exactly the same role. Same level of experience. Same skills. Responsibilities. But one is earning £45k and the other £55k. Why should that mean one gets offered less? Especially when we know women's careers are more likely to have been interrupted by maternity leave, caring responsibilities, career breaks or periods of part-time work. If you've been historically underpaid, basing your next salary on your previous one can simply carry that disadvantage from job to job. And secrecy doesn't exactly help. People can work alongside each other for YEARS doing comparable jobs without knowing there's a significant difference in what they're being paid. You can't question a pay gap you don't know exists. Of course, this doesn't mean everyone doing a similar job must automatically earn exactly the same amount. There can be legitimate reasons for differences in pay - experience, responsibilities, performance, location and other factors. But employers should be able to EXPLAIN those differences. That's the bit I think matters. Pay people based on the role they're doing, the skills and experience they bring and the value of the job. Not what another employer decided they were worth five years ago. And if your pay structures are fair and defensible? Transparency shouldn't be something to fear. 💗 … more

Your employer's PF contribution should not come at the cost of your take-home salary. A change in PF policy should strengthen employees' financial security — not silently reduce their monthly earnings. Following the revision of the EPF wage ceiling, many employees are seeing changes in their salary structures. But an important question needs to be asked: Can an employer shift its own statutory PF contribution burden onto employees by reducing their wages or salary components? Section 12 of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, specifically restricts employers from reducing employees' wages or employment benefits merely because of their liability to pay PF contributions. Consider what employees are experiencing: - Fixed CTC remains unchanged. - Employer PF contribution is adjusted within the existing CTC. - Salary components such as Special Pay are reduced. - Monthly take-home salary goes down. For employees, this is not just a payroll adjustment. It directly affects monthly household budgets, rent, bills, savings and financial commitments. Retirement savings are important. But employees should not be made to bear the employer's statutory contribution through reduced wages. I believe every employer should provide: 1. A transparent revised CTC structure. 2. A clear explanation of employee and employer PF contributions. 3. Written justification for any reduction in salary components. 4. Confirmation that the restructuring complies with applicable labour laws. A social security reform should protect employees without compromising their present financial stability. Employees deserve transparency, fairness and respect for their hard-earned salaries. #EPF #PF #EmployeeRights #LabourLaws #SalaryStructure #CTC #TakeHomeSalary #India … more

Not because of headlines. Because of your people. Do not take my word for it. Take the researchers’. Across 183 studies, people who see their pay as fair are clearly less likely to leave. And people who find the pay process fair trust their employer more (Colquitt et al., 2001). Here is the part most people miss: how you become transparent matters as much as what you show. → Explaining how pay is decided builds trust (SimanTov-Nachlieli & Bamberger, 2021). → Showing who earns what, with no context or explanation, backfires. Below-median staff were 20% more likely to say they were very likely to look for a new job. Being both dissatisfied and likely to look went up by 40% (Card et al., 2012). So the order is: build foundations like job architecture, job levelling and salary bands, and connect them to benchmark data. Calculate the gaps, fix them if they are not justified, and then be transparent. Which would you rather know: what your colleagues earn, or how your own pay was decided? Most pay disparities inside companies don’t happen by malice—they accumulate through years of administrative drift. 📉⚖️ When compensation offers are driven by aggressive candidate negotiations, past salary anchoring, and ad-hoc retention counter-offers, wide pay gaps quietly emerge between colleagues doing the exact same work. The result? Internal distrust, disengaged top talent, and severe legal liability under emerging pay transparency regulations. A truly equitable workplace doesn't rely on assumptions—it runs a Pay Equity Audit: A Practical HR Review of Compensation Gaps: 🔹 The 4 Steps to an Audit-Ready Compensation Structure: 1. Clean the Baseline: Standardize roles by job levels and control for legitimate factors like performance, certifications, and experience. 2. Run Statistical Regressions: Separate the controlled pay gap (equal pay for equal work) from the raw median gap (opportunity and representation gaps). 3. Ring-Fence Remediation Funds: Fix wage gaps through a dedicated equity budget rather than raiding the annual performance merit pool. 4. Fix the Root Causes: Stop asking candidates for past payslips, enforce strict hiring bands, and conduct bi-annual equity checks before appraisal cycles. I used to judge candidates who asked about salary before agreeing to attend an interview. Today, I see things differently. When I first started my career in HR, whenever I called a candidate to invite them for an interview and they asked: "Please, before we proceed, may I know the salary range for this position?" I would honestly think, Are you even interested in the job? Why not attend the interview first? Sometimes, I would interpret the question as a lack of seriousness, unwillingness to work or an excessive focus on money. But years down the line, experience has taught me something different. That candidate wasn't necessarily being difficult. They were being practical. Think about it. A candidate may need to: - Take time off their current job to attend an interview. - Spend money on transportation. - Rearrange personal and family commitments. - Prepare for the interview. - Go through multiple stages of recruitment. Only to eventually discover that the salary is nowhere near their expectations. And let's be honest, employers also invest time and resources in the recruitment process. So, why shouldn't salary alignment be discussed early? I've come to understand that asking about compensation doesn't automatically mean a candidate is only interested in money. It could mean they understand their financial responsibilities, know their worth, have done their research and simply want to establish whether the opportunity is mutually beneficial. As HR professionals, we must understand that recruitment is a two-way process. We assess candidates, but candidates are also assessing us. Transparency about compensation is not a favour to candidates. It is part of creating a professional and respectful recruitment experience. One thing I've learnt throughout my HR journey is that experience doesn't just teach you how to do your job better; sometimes, it challenges the very things you once believed. My question to fellow HR professionals and recruiters: When a candidate asks about the salary range before agreeing to an interview, what's your honest reaction? Do you see it as a red flag or a perfectly reasonable question? Let's have an honest conversation. 👇 #HumanResources #Recruitment #TalentAcquisition #HRLessons #CandidateExperience #PeopleManagement #CareerGrowth … more

Having spent almost six months actively searching for employment and using LinkedIn on an almost daily basis, there are a few things I have noticed that I believe could make the experience better for job seekers. I am sharing these observations constructively, in the hope that they might encourage some positive changes and benefit others going through the same process. 1. Feedback following job applications This is probably my biggest concern. Over the past six months, I have applied for numerous positions, whether through Easy Apply, company websites or external recruitment platforms. In most cases, I receive an automated email confirming that my application has been submitted. However, what often follows is silence. Whether successful or unsuccessful, applicants deserve some form of feedback. A simple acknowledgement that an application has been reviewed and a decision has been made would make a considerable difference. 2. Salary transparency I have noticed that while some employers include salary details or a pay range in their advertisements, many do not. This creates an unnecessary problem for applicants. You find a position that matches your experience and capabilities, submit an application, and potentially progress to a telephone or Teams conversation, only to discover that the salary is considerably below your expectations or financial requirements. That means both the applicant and the employer have invested time in a process that could potentially have been avoided. My suggestion is simple: every job advertisement should include a salary or, at the very least, an indicative salary range. A final thought Looking for employment is already a demanding process, particularly when you have been doing so for an extended period. A little more communication, transparency and consideration from employers and recruiters would make LinkedIn a much better platform for everyone involved. These are simply observations from my own experience, shared in the hope that they might make a difference to someone else's job search. Sometimes, improving the experience doesn't require major changes. It simply requires better communication and a little more consideration. #LinkedIn #JobSearch #Recruitment #CareerOpportunities #SalaryTransparency … more

If you have employees in California, now is a good time to start reviewing your policies, handbooks, and HR practices. A few changes worth having on your radar: 🔹 Bereavement Leave: Expanded coverage to include designated persons who have a family-like relationship with the employee. 🔹 AI & Workplace Surveillance: New restrictions on using AI to predict or recognize employees' emotional states, collect neural data, and surveillance in workplace bathrooms. 🔹 Employee Protections: Expanded protections involving immigration-related retaliation and clarified definitions of sex discrimination, including pregnancy-related conditions. 🔹 Pay Transparency & Reporting: Updated pay data reporting requirements for larger employers. 🔹 AI & Layoff Notices: Additional disclosure requirements when AI or automation contributes to qualifying mass layoffs or terminations. 🔹 Minimum Wage: California's statewide minimum wage will increase to $17.40/hour, bringing the minimum exempt salary threshold to $72,384 annually. Local minimum wages may be higher. 🔹 Stay-or-Pay Agreements: California's restrictions will apply to agreements entered into on or after January 1, 2027, with expanded exceptions. And that's just the highlight reel! There are also updates affecting privacy regulations, agricultural wages, and San Francisco paid parental leave. 💡 My HR takeaway: Don't wait until January to get ahead of compliance. Review your employee handbook, compensation practices, leave policies, and any technology your organization uses to make employment-related decisions. A compliant workplace isn't just about checking boxes. It's about staying informed, protecting your organization, and making sure employees are treated fairly. In my last article I asked why poverty fell in Timor-Leste and admitted I did not know. A reader pushed me to look at the politics rather than the economics, so I went back through the state budget, a World Bank study I worked on, and my own focus groups. What I found: our domestic revenue covers about one-eighth of what the state spends, and our salary bill alone is now bigger than everything the Petroleum Fund can sustainably provide. The oil was not only paying for development. It was paying for our politics — the settlements, the jobs, the contracts that kept the peace after 2006. Both bills now fall due together. And the generation that will carry them told us last year, in six locations, that they cannot get into the room. Disappointing Recruitment Experience with TCS – A Candidate's Perspective I never expected the recruitment process of an organisation like TCS to be this frustrating and disappointing. My interview process (2 technical and 1 managerial) was completed around 9 September 2026. As of 3 November 2026, nearly 2 months (1 month and 25 days) have passed, and I am still dealing with uncertainty around compensation, work location and the recruitment process. After successfully clearing the technical and managerial rounds, I was informed that I had been selected. I submitted the required documents and patiently followed up for the next steps, expecting the process to move forward professionally. However, the compensation discussions became a series of repeated changes. During the initial discussion, I communicated my expectation of a 62.5% hike over my current CTC. Following negotiations, I agreed to a 56.25% hike. I was subsequently informed that this compensation was being considered, and a salary breakup was even shared. Later, I was told that the proposed compensation was not approved. Despite this, I remained flexible and further revised my expectation to a 37.5% hike to keep the opportunity moving forward. After all these discussions and adjustments, the latest proposal communicated to me represents only a 12.5% hike. The work location added to the uncertainty. Kolkata was initially communicated during the discussion, but later I was told that it was tentative and that another location might be required. What is most frustrating is not just the final offer, but the entire recruitment experience. Candidates invest time in preparing for multiple interview rounds, submit personal documents, attend discussions, make career plans and sometimes put other opportunities on hold based on the information communicated by recruiters. Repeated changes, prolonged delays, lack of timely updates and inconsistent communication make the experience extremely disappointing. I run reesmarx europe, and for over 30 years we’ve helped US/ Asian and UK/European companies hire across the UK, Europe and Asia. In that time I’ve noticed the same few rules catch people out, again and again. Here are five worth knowing before you make your first hire: Germany: if you need to let someone go, the letter has to be on paper with a handwritten signature. An email or DocuSign won’t count. Germany: a non-compete only holds up if you pay the person at least half their salary for as long as it runs. Netherlands: if an employee is off sick, you could be paying at least 70% of their salary for up to two years. France: contracts and company policies need to be in French. English-only versions can come back to bite you. Across the EU: new pay transparency rules mean salary ranges up front and no asking candidates what they earned before. Each country is bringing this in on its own timetable, so it’s worth checking where you’re hiring. GDPR. Data rules apply to candidate data too, so even CVs held in a US-based applicant tracking system come under them. None of this should put anyone off. UK/Europe are great markets. But when companies take there first steps over here, getting the people and the local rules right from day one tends to become the hard part. That’s exactly where reesmarx europe help. Before you accept an offer, vet the salary. Finding reliable data can be hard. You can find lots of advice on negotiation. But successful negotiations depend on having accurate data. “Should I negotiate?” isn’t the question. You should! You will never have more leverage. And to do that properly, you need facts. (You can get the quick guide I pulled together on finding salary data here: [link hidden] Here are 8 sources of salary data you can check out to make sure you are aiming for the right number. 1.BLS OEWS - [link hidden] This is the best baseline for nearly any role. It’s survey data from employers, with percentiles (10th through 90th) by occupation, metro area, state, and industry. LIMITS: Reports base wages only, job categories are broad, and the data can be 6 to 18 months old. 2. O*Net - [link hidden] Helpful for finding the right job, job outlook, and ranges by location. Better UX than BLS. LIMITS: Its wage figures come from BLS, and several O*NET titles share one BLS number, so it can lack specificity for some jobs. 3. State Pay Transparency Job Postings Many states require job postings to include current market rates in states. Looking at comparable roles in those states can give you a range. LIMITS: Employers may post wide ranges. Not always translatable to other locations. 4. Glassdoor/Indeed You can find info with company-specific numbers LIMITS: Self-reported. Data can be thin for small companies and niche roles. 5. Payscale. com/[link hidden] These sites adjust pay scales by experience, education and skills LIMITS: Modeled estimates that can look more exact than they are. 6. Levels.fyi Info on total compensation at tech and large employers LIMITS: Overstates pay for most other industries. Often includes equity, so the base may be unclear. 7. H1B/DOL Foreign Labor Certification Data Center [link hidden] and [link hidden] Actual base salaries paid by specific employers, required by law for foreign nationals on H1B visas. Prevailing wages are set at four levels, which is a rough proxy for seniority. LIMITS: Only covers sponsored roles. Skews toward big tech and consulting. 8. Professional Associations These groups often report pay in your own field (legal, healthcare, HR, nonprofit and others) LIMITS: Some survey data requires membership or a fee. The best way to approach finding salary data you can rely on is to check several sites so you can feel confident about the range. Most importantly, get the company’s starting number in writing, and be prepared to negotiate for what you deserve! I pulled together these details for you in a simple two-page pdf. In France, a job's level is negotiated by the industry. In Romania, each employer decides. EU Pay Transparency in Romania | Directive (EU) 2023/970 asks employers to compare work of equal value on four criteria: skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions. France and Romania start from very different places. FRANCE: THE GRID IS NEGOTIATED → Each industry agreement sets a job classification. In metallurgy, since January 2024, every job is scored on 6 criteria and placed in 1 of 18 classes, each with its own minimum salary. → The Labour Code (art. L2241-15) makes industries review their classifications at least every 5 years and remove criteria that could discriminate between women and men. → Group systems (Hay, Mercer, WTW) sit on top, but each grade must map onto an industry class. ROMANIA: THE GRID IS UP TO YOU → COR gives every job a 6-digit code, mandatory in the contract and in REGES-ONLINE. It names the occupation. It says nothing about level or pay. → Industry agreements are rare, and they set a pay floor, not a grid. Banking: 4,500 lei minimum. Construction: 4,582 lei, plus 3% for skilled work. → So grading lives in each company's own pay system, often a global grade imported from headquarters. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR FRENCH GROUPS IN ROMANIA 1. The French grade has been tested against a negotiated, gender-reviewed grid. The Romanian one usually has not. 2. A COR code is not an equal-value group. Jobs with different codes can be work of equal value. 3. The Directive does not hand you a grid either. Article 4 asks that your own pay structures rest on objective, gender-neutral criteria. The EU toolkit on gender-neutral job evaluation (EIGE and the European Commission) is a free starting point: four factors, three methods by company size. My advice: map your group grades to your Romanian jobs now, and test the criteria before the law makes you. If you work in a French group in Romania: do your grades come from France or were they built locally? #PayTransparency #EqualPay #Romania #HR #LabourLaw #JobEvaluation … more

If Harvard can reject brilliant students, why should a business hire someone just for an excellent CV? What exactly qualifies you for a role? Let me share a story. Sometime ago, we shared an opening for a female mathematics tutor. One lady applied, and her application was impressive. Excellent CV. Very good introduction video. Plus certification in teaching mathematical concepts using pictures and visual representations. Now, this caught my attention. At BKB Learning Hub, we work with children who learn differently. So, this lady looked like someone who could add value. We shortlisted her, and I scheduled a call with her. During our discussion, I learned she was already teaching in a physical school. And please, don't get me wrong. There is nothing wrong with teaching in a physical school. In fact, I intend to own one. But I needed to understand her schedule. So I asked about her availability in the evenings. She explained that she already had some tutoring commitments after school. Now, think about this. You finish your regular teaching job around 4 p.m. You take additional lessons between 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. Then you prepare for another class at 9, 10 or even 11 p.m. because you are teaching children in the United States. Depending on your schedule, you could finish teaching at 1a.m or 2 a.m. And then? You still have to wake up around 5:30 or 6 a.m. to prepare for your regular teaching job. Ah! You see, teaching is mental work. It requires concentration, patience, preparation, and keen observation. You are not just opening a textbook and reading to a child. How do you consistently give a child that level of attention when you are already exhausted? Now, you might say, "But Mrs Light, don't you also work at night?" Of course I do! There are nights I finish working at 3 a.m., 4 a.m., sometimes even 6 a.m. On some crazy days, I don't sleep until 8 a.m. But here is the difference. I have the flexibility to sleep during the day. If I finish working at 4 a.m., I can arrange my schedule to get enough rest. Many of our tutors also have that flexibility. They can teach at night and rest during the day. So, after considering her commitments and the demands of the role, I decided, not her. Why? Because I wasn't convinced that she would give our learners the attention they deserve. Then, sometime ago, I came across a write-up asking if a teacher should be rejected because they have a 9 to 5 job. And I thought. Does being qualified automatically mean you are suitable for every opportunity? A good CV or an excellent interview? Because at the end of the day, we are not just hiring someone who knows mathematics. We are hiring someone who will be responsible for a child's learning. Now, over to you. Would you say I was right to turn her down, or should I have given her a chance? I genuinely want to read your comments.

posts.text: November QS Market Predictions | What’s next for the Quantity Surveying market? As we head into November, there are a few trends I expect to see shaping the Quantity Surveying market across Australia. My predictions: 1. Demand for experienced QS professionals will remain competitive. Particularly those who can confidently manage projects from feasibility and cost planning through to final account. 2. Businesses will become more strategic with hiring. Rather than simply increasing headcount, consultancies will be looking for individuals who can add immediate value, strengthen existing teams and support future project pipelines. 3. Salary expectations will continue to be a key conversation. With experienced QS professionals in demand, businesses will need to ensure their remuneration packages reflect the current market. 4. Technical ability won't be enough. Communication, commercial awareness, client management and the ability to build strong relationships will continue to separate good QS professionals from great ones. 5. The lead-up to 2027 will drive hiring conversations. Businesses that start planning their workforce requirements now will be better positioned to secure quality talent ahead of the new year. One thing remains consistent: the best Quantity Surveyors are rarely on the market for long. For consultancies, understanding the market and having the right conversations early will be key to attracting and retaining the right people. What's one trend you're expecting to see in the QS market heading into the new year? #QuantitySurveying #Construction #Recruitment #CostManagement #AustralianConstruction

posts.text: An Employer of Record (EOR) can make a remote architect legally employable. It cannot tell you whether that architect can deliver. For Architecture, Engineering, Construction (AEC), and Development firms, hiring remotely is less about the contract and more about the work. The hard questions are: ✔ Finding the right professional. A Revit architect, a Building Information Modeling (BIM) coordinator, and a quantity surveyor are not interchangeable. ✔ Vetting by people who know the work, not just a CV. ✔ Time zone overlap with your United States (US) project team. ✔ Embedding the professional in your systems, processes, and meetings. As EOR fees fall, the real difference in a remote hire comes down to the person you choose and how well they fit your team. At ADDMORE Services, we source, vet, and engage pre-qualified professionals across Latin America, South Africa, and the Philippines. Your team directs the daily work, and we handle the rest. posts.text: I read about a hiring event this week that worked very differently from anything I have seen so far. On Monday, the Philippines' Department of Migrant Workers and the Croatian Employment Service signed recruitment procedures and opened 785 hospitality jobs in Croatia to Filipino workers, for roles like hotel staff, chefs, waiters and housekeeping. Nine Croatian hotel employers came to interview applicants in person, and 943 people were shortlisted. The agreement covers how the recruiting works along with legal and security protections for the workers who go. What I keep thinking about is how much of the work I would have expected an agency to handle, like shortlisting candidates and setting the ground rules, was taken on by two governments here. I am still very new to international recruiting, so I honestly do not know whether this is common or unusual. For those of you who have placed people across borders, does an agreement like this make your job easier because the rules are clear, or does it take away work that used to go to recruiters?

posts.text: Am I about to confuse all of you with my different posts? Maybe? No, I think you're all smarter than that. 😉 Niche-ing, fitting into a box was never really my thing. OK, the umbrella is HOSPITALITY & YACHTING, and underneath that come many things: • Service & Hospitality Coaching • Yacht Crew Training & Education • Communication & Leadership And so on... And collaborating with others in the industry will always be part of what I do. Which brings me to this CV workshop, in collaboration with Yacht Maritime. Lucy spent years working in yachting and now works in recruitment. We got talking, and the topic of how poor so many CVs are here came up. For years, I was also responsible for hiring yacht crew for our fleet, and honestly, some of the CVs were shockingly basic. A Word document or Europass CV might get you by locally, but it doesn't necessarily cut it in the international yachting scene. This isn't a judgement, it's just a reality. Your CV is your first impression. Your passport to the industry. And a lot of people are missing out on opportunities simply because their CV isn't showcasing them properly. The good news? That's an easy fix, WHEN you know how. Continuing to raise the standard in hospitality and yachting is what I am about. And that will come in big and small ways. From conversations and networking, to workshops like this, to my private education and consulting work. So, if you're new to yachting, looking to break into the international market, or an experienced crew member who knows their CV could do with some attention, join us at our workshop in Split. This one will be particularly valuable if you're looking to take that next step in your yachting career. New season. New opportunities. Better CV. DM to learn more.

posts.text: Three months unemployed, and I’m still looking for my next opportunity. These past few months have been a rollercoaster. Interviews come and go. Some go so well that I walk out thinking, “This could be it.” I get invited to the next round, then the next, and I let myself hope. Then the email arrives: “We’ve decided to move forward with other candidates.” Or sometimes: “We’ve decided to pause hiring for this role for now.” I’d be lying if I said it doesn’t sting. Every rejection is a little disappointing, and the bank account is bleeding a little more each month. But I’ve learned that every one of them tells a story too. It’s rarely about ability. More often it’s about fit, timing, or what a company needs at that moment. Sometimes the role itself changes before anyone is hired. Each interview has sharpened how I tell my story, and each “no” has pointed me closer to the right “yes”. So I’m not giving up. I’ll keep applying, keep learning, and keep showing up.
