posts.text: “We can discuss the work arrangement at the interview.” That sentence can leave an important part of your hiring brief unresolved. For Singapore employers, workspace planning affects more than office capacity. It shapes who considers the role, what recruiters screen for and whether the eventual offer matches the candidate’s expectations. Before sourcing begins, clarify three things. Where will the work happen? Specify the actual work location, expected office attendance and any travel between sites. If hybrid work is available, explain the arrangement and any conditions. “Flexible” should mean something both sides can understand. What does the role need? A client-facing employee, an operations coordinator and a specialist doing focused work may need different setups. Define the requirements around customer access, collaboration, equipment and privacy. Connect attendance expectations to the work involved. Does the setup support your hiring plan? Separate the vacancy you need to fill now from future headcount plans. Confirm who the new hire reports to, where onboarding happens and whether the workspace and equipment will be ready for the intended start date. Then carry those decisions through the recruitment process: CLARIFY Put the location, work arrangement, role outcomes and reporting line into one agreed brief. SHORTLIST Assess candidates against the actual requirements, including whether the working arrangement suits them. DECIDE Keep interviewers aligned, respond promptly and make sure the offer reflects what was discussed. For example, if a role requires daily attendance at an Ubi office and regular client visits, explain both upfront. Candidates can then assess the opportunity with a clearer understanding of the job. If the arrangement is still being decided, say so clearly. Hyer Talents supports Singapore employers with structured hiring briefs, relevant shortlists and responsive interview coordination. A clearer brief gives everyone a better basis for the next decision. Hiring in Singapore? #hiring Senior Audit Associate

Apply here: https://lnkd.in/gTqCiQiC

Job Description If youre going to leave a firm youre perfectly happy at, the next one needs to give you a few good reasons.  This one does.  Theyre an Indianapolis-based CPA firm of around 40 people, currently growing and moving into a bigger space. Theyve had opportunities to grow much faster through mergers, but that isnt really what they want.  Theyd rather keep the feel of a smaller firm and grow by hiring good people.  And right now, they particularly need experienced people in the middle of the team.  As an Audit Senior, youd work across a varied client base including construction, manufacturing, nonprofit, and public sector organizations. Youll be involved across engagements, working directly with clients and taking on more responsibility as you progress.  Its a good place for someone who wants to keep learning without feeling like theyre one of 100 Seniors all waiting for the same promotion.  They do want people in the office and on site for certain engagements, particularly because they put a lot of emphasis on training. But theyre sensible about what flexibility actually means.  Busy season is around 55 hours, and Saturdays can be worked from home. Outside of busy season, youre generally back to a normal 40-hour week.  If youve got children, a doctors appointment or just something you need to sort during the day, theyll work around it. Nobody needs to make their dentist appointment sound like a national emergency.  There are some good practical benefits too.  They cover 90% of your parking costs, theres a workout facility in the building and food available in the canteen. Theyve also introduced a 30 minute mental health break during the working day.  One of the more unusual benefits is what happens when you work additional hours.  Once you go beyond their annual hours threshold, extra hours can start converting into additional vacation time. Around 200 hours above that threshold works out at roughly another week of PTO.  Theyre looking for someone with solid public accounting audit experience whos ready to step into a Senior level role. You dont need to have your CPA already, although itll become important if you want to progress into management later on.  You might be quite comfortable where you are.  But if you could move somewhere that stays relatively small, gives you room to progress, and makes busy season a little easier to live with, it might be worth seeing what else is out there.  If youre just browsing the job boards and you havent dusted off your resume yet, thats not a problem. If youve read this advert and youre unsure whether to apply because you dont have every bit of experience listed, Id still encourage you to apply. CLPHA is pleased to announce the hiring for three positions. Isaac Dozier MBA Dozier is the new director of Housing Is, CLPHA’s pioneering initiative to align health, housing and education efforts to improve the lives of public housing residents. Lesley Freiman and Chandler Ian Wilkins, PhD, have joined CLPHA as senior policy analysts. They will be responsible for researching and developing CLPHA’s positions on a range of policies including public housing, Housing Choice Vouchers, preservation and redevelopment, and economic mobility.

“We are thrilled to welcome Isaac, Lesley, and Chandler to the CLPHA team,” said La Shelle Dozier, CEO of CLPHA. “They each bring deep expertise to their positions. Their energy and enthusiasm for advancing CLPHA’s mission to serve our PHA members and their residents will be a tremendous asset as we navigate the challenges facing public and affordable housing. Please join me in welcoming them to the team.”

Isaac Dozier comes to Housing Is from the U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development (HUD), where he led more than $100 million in public-private partnership initiatives connecting public housing authorities, developers, and community organizations to HUD’s redevelopment priorities as the Senior Project Manager, Neighborhood and Community Investment for the Jobs Plus Program. Before HUD, Isaac was the Director of Community Development for the Housing Authority of the City of Fort Myers, Florida, Regional Vice President of Urban Strategies, Inc., and Director of Client Services for the Housing Authority of New Orleans. Isaac also previously served in the U.S. Army and holds an MBA from American Inter-Continental University and a BA from the University of Texas at El Paso.

Lesley Freiman is a policy and strategy leader with more 15 years of experience advancing housing stability, economic mobility, community health and family well-being through cross-sector partnerships, implementation support, organizational learning, and capacity building. Prior to joining CLPHA, Lesley was an associate at Abt Global, where she directed research, evaluation, and technical assistance initiatives for federal and nonprofit clients. Lesley holds a Master of Public Policy from the University of Michigan's Ford School and a bachelor's degree from Brown University.

Chandler Ian Wilkins, PhD, is a housing policy researcher with experience studying the intersection of federal housing policy, disaster recovery, and community resilience. He previously served as a research associate at the Urban Institute, where he led and contributed to federally and philanthropically funded research on housing resilience, disaster preparedness, flood mitigation in subsidized housing, and equitable community resilience planning. Chandler holds a PhD in Urban and Regional Science and a Master of Urban Planning from Texas A&M University, as well as a Bachelor of Science in Community and Regional Planning from Iowa State University.

I've always believed that skills can be taught, but attitude and life experience are a different matter. People who've faced significant challenges in life can bring so much to the workplace. Resilience, determination, resourcefulness and often a completely different way of looking at things. And that's something I think businesses underestimate. Someone looking at a challenge through a different set of eyes might just come up with a brilliant idea or a better way of doing something that nobody else had thought of. That's how businesses grow too! Throughout my career I've seen what happens when people are given an opportunity, trusted and supported to develop (and I've been fortunate enough to have been given that chance myself when life wasn't looking too good!) I do wonder whether we sometimes get so caught up in someone's qualifications and previous experience that we miss the person and their potential. After all, isn't that part of being a great leader? Seeing what someone could become, rather than just what they've done so far. I suspect there's some extraordinary talent out there that simply doesn't come wrapped in the CV we're expecting! … more

Connecting workforce identity checks with cybersecurity makes the risk much clearer for businesses. Explaining how verification works across the hiring journey can help decision-makers understand both the threat and the value of a proactive solution.

The claim that governments are sounding the alarm about workforce fraud is concerning, especially given the rise in deepfake technology. As someone who's seen how easily identity verification can be bypassed with synthetic identity fraud, I'm curious about Deel's approach to audit-ready evidence - do you use behavioral biometrics or multi-factor identity validation at scale? The move from HR problem to board-level security risk suggests we're seeing an increase in coordinated attacks targeting hiring workflows, which is something our engineering team has been monitoring closely. … more

Treating the hiring pipeline as an extension of the cybersecurity attack surface is a critical shift. Deepfakes, proxy candidates, and identity fraud have made traditional background checks obsolete for distributed teams. Embedding continuous identity verification directly into global onboarding is the only way to protect cross-border systems. 🔒

To be fair, the JD does mention product-suite ownership, business economics and platform thinking. But as a candidate, I'd still ask: “Which specific product or product suite will I own in my first 6 months?” A very reasonable question before investing time in the process.
My favourite JD decoding rule: If you cannot identify the customer, product boundary and success metric, don't start tailoring your resume yet. First understand what you're applying for. 😂
This is the difference between applying to a job title and positioning for an actual mandate. That's what I help PMs decode through personalised JD X-RAY sessions. 📌 [link hidden]

The "own a suite of products" line is the tell — when a JD can't name the product, the scope is whatever's on fire that quarter. The question I always had to ask a recruiter was who actually owns the P&L and the roadmap call, because "cross-functional leadership" in a JD usually means you get the accountability without the authority. Your four-point checklist is the right filter; I'd add a fifth — who can say no to a request and make it stick. In my experience, that's the difference between a PM and a very well-paid order-taker.

[name hidden] Ryan, that fifth question is gold. 👏 Accountability without decision authority is one of the biggest traps hidden inside senior PM roles. I'd go one step further: Who has the final call when priorities conflict, and who backs that decision? Because a PM's real mandate isn't measured by how many things they own, but by the decisions they're empowered to make. 🎯

What will MasterCard do when Visa Network has ICICI onboarded from so long ? MasteCard issued HDFC ? And the Rupay network is prepaid as well as credit card our very own and set up with UPI and NPCI in mind ? What is MasterCard trying to achieve ?
That repeat visit point is the real test, Bhawana. A product parents trust once is the one they come back to without thinking.

👉The phrase I'd investigate in this JD: “Partner with worldwide Payments, Subscriptions, Personalization and App Experience teams.” My question: Who owns the final trade-off when local customer needs conflict with global platform priorities? That's where the real mandate becomes visible.

✅️ A useful interview question: “Which decisions can this PM make independently, which require global alignment, and which are owned by another product team?” Three answers. Three very different operating models.

📍Here's the candidate exercise: A local payment method improves conversion in India but adds complexity to a global payments platform. What would you evaluate before prioritising it? Customer value. Conversion. Cost. Reuse. Operational complexity. That's the product judgement behind the job title.

dataHash.scope: Canonical sorted-key UTF-8 JSON of {posts,comments}, compact separators

hashes.recordsScope: Canonical sorted-key UTF-8 JSON of {posts,comments}, compact separators

ageCoverage.definition: ageDays is exposure at collection, not age as of today. Exact source dates and dates derived from relative labels are separated.

analysisRule.expression: !isDuplicate && rawSourceTextLength >= 80 && likes !== null && commentsCount !== null && batch !== 'B7'
analysisRule.textLengthBasis: Original CSV post_text before anonymisation; whitespace counted, matching legacy builder.

meta.textFeaturePolicy: All six current text features are recalculated by the browser's current rules from the anonymised full text, rather than copied from the legacy five-signal aggregates. Link presence alone does not establish an application path. Regex coding needs human review.

datePolicy.exact: Source post_time, compared with collected_at at calendar-day precision.
datePolicy.relative: Parsed minute/hour/day/week time_label. ageDays is retained; publishedAt remains null because the exact date/time is unknown.
datePolicy.missing: No usable observation; no date or age is invented. LI00030 has a source publication date one day after collection; both age and publication date are suppressed.
datePolicy.commentCollectedAt: Inherited from linked post collection timestamp; comment export has no collection timestamp. Unlinked comments remain null.

privacy.policy: No author fields. Known author/commenter names, emails, phone candidates, body URLs and contact handles are replaced. Only LinkedIn source-post URLs are retained in url. No text truncation.
privacy.salaryPolicy: Currency amounts, pay-unit amounts, and unlabelled four-plus-digit salary ranges are preserved when not explicitly phone-labelled.

limitations: Convenience sample of visible public LinkedIn hiring-related posts; not representative of the labour market.
Visible likes and comments are observations at collection, not applicants, hires, reach, or causal hiring effectiveness.
Different posting ages, occupations, search lanes, and collection batches can confound engagement comparisons.
Comment rows are the collected visible comment layer, not all comments counted by LinkedIn; five empty bodies remain present.
Source post_text can itself be clipped by the captured public page; this export preserves all supplied text and adds no length truncation.
Posts without LinkedIn links remain in the snapshot; their source page cannot be opened from the supplied master data.
Automated regex job families and text signals are coding aids and may contain classification error.
Redaction can affect text-signal detection; original contact values are intentionally unavailable to the public browser dataset.
All current text features use anonymised text and current browser rules; link presence alone does not establish an application path, and rule matches need human review.
Seven newly supplied rows could not pass the website validation rules and remain excluded from the bundled working baseline.

The 2026-11-20 working baseline merges the original frozen sample with the education, manufacturing, construction, real-estate, hospitality, operations/administration and partial healthcare collections.
The healthcare source is a partial batch stopped at LinkedIn login or verification; it has 89 raw records and does not represent a completed 500-record collection.

The finance and insurance import contains 85 approved posts and 44 linked comments from a 160-candidate batch. Search URLs requested the past month, but the collection summary could not confirm that filter automatically for every query.
The public-sector/non-profit import added 67 dated posts derived from confirmed LinkedIn post IDs and 49 linked comments; one unique candidate without a confirmed source ID was excluded.

roleMigration.note: Known industry codes take priority over job-function wording. Education, manufacturing, construction and other sector markers are also recognized from keywords and post text.
